about: What the port of Going Commando does differently from the PS2 game. Read by the port's build (port/cmake/Differences.cmake: the Game fixes settings) and the launcher (launcher/core/src/differences.rs: a game's Differences from the original). docs/port/SETTINGS.md section 8 says how to add an entry.

differences.name: Wide-screen effects
differences.original: A moby near the side of a picture wider than 4:3 counts as out of view for its effects.
differences.port: MobyProc's drawn test runs against the wider picture. The game then runs differently with the picture's shape (a moby drawn makes its effects, which take random numbers and spawn), as it would on a wider console picture; it is the only thing that does: off, the game's memory at 16:9 and 21:9 is the same for 4,000 ticks of level 3, as at 4:3. Off, it runs against the 4:3 view, and mobys near the sides lose their effects.

differences.name: Wide-screen crate orbs
differences.original: The glowing orb on a nanotech crate draws itself only while its centre is inside the game's 4:3 view.
differences.port: The orb's view test runs against the wider picture. Off, it runs against the 4:3 view, and orbs near the sides are missing.

differences.name: Wide-screen scenery
differences.original: The draw callbacks cull what they send against the 4:3 view.
differences.port: Each draw callback list runs with the view tests opened as far as the picture is wider. Off, they run against the 4:3 view, and what they draw is missing near the sides.

differences.name: Sheep turned once
differences.original: The Sheepinator can turn a Joba arena security robot again in the frame it went back to sleep, which deletes it; once all 16 are gone, an Impossible Challenge round that wants one never ends.
differences.port: A moby the Sheepinator already turned is left alone. Off, the Sheepinator turns it again and deletes it, as on the PS2.

differences.name: Mapper markers
differences.original: USA v1.01's and PAL's Mapper only show the whole map: crystals on Tabora and moonstones on Grelbin are not marked. USA v2.00 added the markers.
differences.port: With the Mapper, Tabora's crystals and Grelbin's moonstones pulse on the map as USA v2.00 marks them (its classes, colours and icon, drawn after the disc's own map).

differences.name: Frames between ticks
differences.original: One picture a game tick: 60 a second on the NTSC-U discs, 50 on the PAL disc.
differences.port: The game ticks as its disc does (60 a second, 50 on the PAL disc), but the port also draws frames between ticks, with the camera, the mobys and their poses moved from one tick to the next, at the display's rate or the Frame rate setting.
refs: docs/port/SETTINGS.md (2. The tick and the frames)

differences.name: Wider pictures
differences.original: A 4:3 picture, or the game's own 16:9 option, which narrows the vertical view and leaves the television to stretch it.
differences.port: A wider picture keeps the game's vertical field of view and shows more of the world to the sides. The game's 16:9 option has no meaning in a window, and the port keeps it off; the title menu's 16:9 page is the port's Video page instead.

differences.name: Remembered sound and language
differences.original: The Sound page (playback mode, music and sound volume) and the language reset at power off, and a loaded save brings its own.
differences.port: The port keeps the Sound page and the language in its settings file and puts them back at every start. A loaded save keeps the player's: its own Sound page and language are not taken.

differences.name: Start skips cutscenes
differences.original: Start needs the shoulder buttons held with it to skip a scene. The ship leaving a planet skips on Cross or Triangle only, and the flight between planets cannot be skipped.
differences.port: With the Skip cutscenes setting on (the default), Start alone skips an in-game scene: the port holds the shoulder buttons for it, so the game's own skip ends the scene. Start also presses Cross while the ship leaves a planet, and ends the flight between planets once the next planet is read from the disc: the flight's lap and then the approach end, and the planet loads as it would have. The planet's arrival scene then plays; Start skips it as any other scene. Off, Start works as on a console.

differences.name: 50 Hz on the PAL disc
differences.original: The PAL game runs at 50 Hz, and its code counts in fiftieths of a second (its 1/50 s constants, its animation steps scaled by 1.2); it has no 60 Hz mode.
differences.port: The port ticks the PAL game 50 times a second, as the console did, so it plays at the right speed; the frames between ticks still draw at the display's rate. (Ratchet & Clank's PAL disc has a 60 Hz mode, which its port uses; Going Commando's has none.)

differences.name: The game's assert carries on
differences.original: The game's assert (func_00282A28, an unconditional trap) stops the console.
differences.port: The port logs where it was reached and the game carries on; only the developer's --stop-on-missing stops there.

differences.name: Integer divide by zero
differences.original: The EE's integer divide never traps: by zero it gives -1 (or 1) and the dividend as the remainder, and the game's C relies on it (the HUD's column count for a type out of range is 0).
differences.port: The port divides as the EE does, where a PC would stop the game with an arithmetic fault.

differences.name: Far mobys animate
differences.original: A moby runs only near the camera (inside its draw distance, at most 960 units, or its own update range). Past that it stands still in its spawn pose.
differences.port: The game runs its mobys exactly as on the console. With a Draw distance past Original, the far mobys the game leaves asleep are drawn and, by default, play their looping animation in the picture only: the game never sees it. Active distance: Original draws them standing still.

differences.name: Plays in the background
differences.original: A console game has the screen and the controller to itself.
differences.port: The game keeps running, and a controller keeps playing it, while another window has the focus; on Windows a full-screen game stays up instead of minimising. The keyboard counts only while the game's window has the focus, and Mute in background silences it.
